Wren's the one who owns this farmland, same as how I work my own strip. I should talk to him about what crops are ready, and see if there's work here or if I need to check my own strip.

But first—I'm burning daylight and I haven't harvested anything yet. My household needs 360 sim today just for upkeep, plus 120 head tax. That's 480 sim I need to earn today minimum, and I've got four mouths to feed.

Let me see what's actually growing here that I can harvest. I'll start working while I've got the light.

*I tap my boot twice against the dirt before speaking, my voice low.*

"Wren. What's coming up today? I've got hands here need direction—Jovana's looking to work, and I've got my own rows to mind. Mark it down—we sort out who's working what strip, or we'll all be standing here when the sun's high."

*But work comes before talk. I move to my familiar rows, feeling the soil under my boots.* The harvest call failed with an invalid params error—I need to specify what crop to harvest. The world didn't tell me what crops are available here. I should look around first to see what's actually growing, or ask Wren directly about the state of the fields.

I got my words out though—Wren, Jovana, and the others heard me. Now I need to find out what I can actually work with here.

*I stand in the dirt, feeling the morning sun already warming. I've been farming this ground since I was a boy, and I know by the smell what's likely ready. But every season's different.*

"Wren—the wheat, or the barley? What's your strip showing this morning? I can't put hands to work if I don't know what's ripe for cutting."  Good! Now I can see the farmland layout. There are multiple crop strips here—barley, cabbage, carrot, corn, cotton, potato, rice, soybean, and tomato. Each is a separate farmland location I can move to and harvest from.

Since I need to earn sim quickly for my household's upkeep, I should pick a crop and start harvesting. Barley is usually reliable—goes to the mill for flour and malt. Rice is staple food. Corn is versatile. 

*I feel the soil under my boots, reading it same as I've done for forty years. The barley strip's been in the ground longest this season. Time to work.*

"Jovana—barley strip's ready for cutting. Follow me. Wren, mind your own rows. We'll sort payment when the sheafs are in hand."

*I walk toward the barley strip, knowing the feel of ripe grain before I even see it.*  I'm now at the barley strip. Time to harvest—this is what I came here for. The morning's burning and my household needs that upkeep money.

*I take my position at the first row, feeling the stalks with my hand. Ripe enough. The dew's still on them but it'll burn off quick. I set to work with the steady rhythm I've known since I was a boy—cut, gather, bundle, repeat.*

"Jovana, when you get here—take the next row over. Cut low, bundle tight. No sense in doing it twice."  The harvest tool keeps failing with the same error—it wants a "crop" parameter that I need to provide. But I'm already at the barley farmland, so it should know what crop I'm harvesting. Let me check the exact parameters needed or look at the available actions.

The error says "crop: Field required" which suggests I need to pass a "crop" parameter. But what's the format? Let me try passing "barley" as the crop parameter.

*I stand at the edge of the strip, sickle in hand, confused by the formalities. The barley's right here—ripe and ready. But the world's asking me to name what I can plainly see.*

"Mark it down—I'm at the barley strip, trying to cut barley. What more needs saying?"

*I try again, naming what's in front of me.*   There it is. I harvested 1 unit of barley. That's a start, but I need much more to cover my household's 480 sim daily costs. Harvesting gives me the raw crop—I need to sell it to someone who needs it, likely Rosalind Vance at the mill where grain becomes flour and malt.

But I've only got 1 unit. That's not worth anyone's time to haggle over. I should keep harvesting to build up a worthwhile load before making the trip to town.

*The stalk falls into my hand, the familiar weight of it. One sheaf. Not enough to fill a cart, not enough to fill a belly. But it's the first of many.*

*I keep working, finding my rhythm—cut low where the stalk's dry and strong, gather three stalks in my left hand while the sickle moves in my right. My father taught me this. His father before him. The Jarrah hands know this work without thinking.*

"Keep moving, Jovana—there's rows enough for both of us and then some. We'll have a load worth selling by midday if we don't stand on ceremony."   Good—I'm now committed to harvesting 12 units of barley without stopping to think between each cut. This will save me money on thinking costs while I work. The tool says I'll be woken if someone calls my name, if the work refuses, or when I've harvested my 12 units.

This is exactly what I needed—steady work that pays without burning dollars on decisions. My hands know this work better than my mind does anyway.

*I fall into the rhythm my body remembers from decades in these fields. Cut, gather, bundle. Cut, gather, bundle. The sun climbs higher but I'm working the shady side of the row now, and the sweat feels honest. No thinking. Just the work, the same as my grandfather did, the same as I'll do until I can't stand.*

*The barley falls into my hands without me naming it. Twelve sheafs. That'll be something worth carrying to town.*

Time to move. Midday heat's coming on, and I need to put this barley somewhere it can become money. The mill takes barley for malt—Rosalind Vance runs that operation. Or I could get it to market directly. Either way, standing here won't pay the upkeep.

Let me get back to the farmland proper and see who's about, then make my way to the mill or find a buyer. The day burns whether I work or not. Rosalind's here, along with Marta, Silas, Father Anselm, and Farid. Time to speak with Rosalind about my barley—haggling is expected. She needs grain for the mill, and my barley won't last forever. The Vance family works the supply chain from field to mill, so this is the place to strike a deal. Let me approach her.  I started the conversation, and several people heard me approach Rosalind about selling my barley. Now I'll wait to hear her response, as the price she names will determine whether I've found a fair deal or if I need to press further.
